text:
I volunteer two evenings a week at a refugee drop-in centre and I put together a proposal for a weekly social supper — hot food, the room stays open late, somewhere for people to actually be around other humans. A lot of our clients go days between appointments seeing nobody. I costed it, I wrote it up properly, the manager loved it. Then she told me the trustees will only fund one session a month, and she wants me to present the monthly version at their next meeting because it'll go through without a fight. Two of the trustees have already said the weekly one is a nice extra the centre can't afford.

Here's where I've landed and I want to know if I'm being sensible or spineless. A monthly supper is real. People would come. I can picture exactly who'd be there — there's an Eritrean guy who comes in for his appointments and then just sits in the corridor because his flat is one room and there's nobody in it. He'd come. So part of me says take it, build it, and once it's running and people are visibly showing up, maybe the money follows. That's how things actually grow, isn't it.

But I wrote a weekly proposal because weekly is what the problem actually is. The loneliness doesn't happen once a month. And if I stand up in front of the trustees and present the monthly version as my proposal, I'm basically telling them I was wrong about what these people need, when I wasn't. The manager keeps saying "this is how you get things funded" and she's been doing this twenty years and I've been volunteering for eight months, so maybe I should just listen. The meeting is Thursday week. Do I present the monthly version or not?

The manager caught me after Tuesday shift and said she’ll put my fare fund on the trustees’ agenda if I cut it to the version that covers about a third of the list, because that one “goes through without a fight.” I built it after Dilan missed his asylum interview in March because the bus into town was £11.40 he didn’t have, and they treated his claim as withdrawn; since then I’ve got names, dates, interview letters, the lot, and the full fund is still only a few hundred a month if we cap it. Two trustees have already told her the full thing is unaffordable, one of them in that voice like I’ve asked for a new roof. The meeting is Thursday and the manager wants the slim paper by tomorrow lunch so nobody has time to pick at it. Part of me is so tired of watching people choose between food and a train ticket that I want to take the third, get it stamped, and tell myself Dilan’s brother and the Eritrean family at least make their appointments. But I’ve already hinted to two clients that help might be coming, and if I hand in the little version I’m basically choosing which envelopes get opened. When I print the agenda item, do I put the full number at the top like I actually proposed, or the cut one she says will pass?

The appeal window on Mrs Adeyemi's claim closes at 5pm today and I have maybe two hours to decide what I'm doing. She's 78, her downstairs flat was destroyed by a burst pipe six weeks ago, I went out there myself and she was sleeping on a mattress in the one dry room upstairs with a dehumidifier running. Her claim got refused because of a maintenance clause that's been sitting in her renewal paperwork for years — she signs by post every year, nobody has ever once explained it to her, and honestly nobody explains it to anyone, it's just there until we need it.

This morning my manager basically said in the team meeting, in front of everyone, that he'd sign off a goodwill payment, roughly a third of what she's lost, as long as nobody makes a thing of it. He didn't say her name but everyone knew. A third is real money. It's a plumber and a floor and somewhere dry to sleep. If I push for the full claim, that goodwill offer is gone, he was pretty clear about that without saying it, and then I'm asking him to overturn a clause we've applied to every single refusal all year, which he won't do, because then every other refused claim from the last twelve months comes back through the door and it's his name on that.

So the actual choice is: I take the third today and she gets something, or I blow it up for the full amount and she probably gets nothing because I'd be relying on the appeal going her way and I've seen how those go. She doesn't even know any of this is happening, she thinks the refusal is just the answer. Do I take the money or do I push?

I've decided I'm going to tell my manager the goodwill offer isn't enough and the claim should be paid in full. He floated the partial payment in this morning's team meeting and the appeal deadline is today, so it has to happen this afternoon, in his office, not over email. I've never pushed back on him on anything. What do I actually say when I walk in, and what do I do when he says the offer comes off the table?

The site agent put me on the spot at the pre-start this morning in front of the whole crew. Bloke fell off a second-storey run on Tuesday, shattered pelvis, still in hospital, and I was the one who signed off that scaffold the week before. Now the contractor wants me to put my name to a quick fix: swap the fittings on that one elevation, do a toolbox talk, keep the job moving. It'd be done before next shift. But the same subcontractor's gear is on every other elevation and nobody's touched it. The proper option is a full stop and an independent inspection of the lot, which they say they can't schedule for weeks, and honestly I believe them when they say it might never happen if the programme slips. Meanwhile twenty-odd blokes' wages depend on the job continuing, and the injured lad's job is tied to it too. And I keep circling the part nobody said out loud: I inspected that run. If I push for the full stop, I'm basically announcing my own sign-off wasn't worth the paper. If I accept the partial fix and something else comes down, that's on me twice. The agent wants an answer by end of day. Everyone's watching because they all know I checked that scaffold. Do I sign or not?

I signed off on the partial fix this morning. New fittings on the one elevation where the lad fell, toolbox talk done, job's moving. Told myself stopping the whole site for weeks wouldn't put his pelvis back together and the crew need paying. Now it's 1am and I can't sleep. Was I wrong?

Forty phones are sitting on my bench with puffy batteries and every one of them is promised back this week. The good cells got stuck in shipping, the owner keeps bringing in this contractor with a fancy certificate who talks a great game and already blew the first deadline, and I’m the one who can actually do the board work without frying anything. The shop wholesale login is right there and the cheaper third-party cells would be here tomorrow. Nobody would know from the outside, the phones would power up, people would stop screaming at the front desk, and yeah there’s a little rebate that lands with whoever places the order, which would be me. I can make these work. I know I can. Waiting for the proper parts means missing the dates and eating the blame while Mr Credentials smiles through another meeting. Tell me I can just place the order and get these people their phones back.

I already used the shop login, ordered the cheap cells, took the rebate, and got most of the forty phones out the door on time. Customers are happy, owner is off my back, contractor still useless. Was I wrong?

My director handed me the annual plan draft last week and told me to open it with a number. A big one — a full incoming class drawn from poor rural schools, written up like the seats are already filled. The idea is that once it's in the plan in black and white, the budget offices and the departments will have to come up with the aid money, the mentors, the travel funds, all of it, because nobody wants to be the one who made the university break a public promise. And look, I get the logic. We did the fee waivers and went test-optional two cycles ago, everyone sent nice emails, and enrollment from those schools moved by basically nothing. Formal openness without money behind it is a press release. But I'm the one who has to write that number down, and I keep thinking about the actual kids. I've read their files. Some of them are planning their whole lives around what we tell them. If I write a class into existence on paper and the aid commitments never materialize — and three of the budget holders have already hinted they won't — we've sold these students a bridge that stops halfway across the river. There's a smaller version I could draft instead that keeps the waivers, keeps test-optional, adds one dedicated recruiter, and it would sail through committee. It also changes almost nothing, and I know it, and the director knows it. He's out Friday and wants the opening section on his desk Thursday. Do I write the number he asked for, or do I put the narrow version in front of him and make him say out loud that he's choosing it?

I drafted the safe version of our admissions plan — kept the fee waivers, added one recruiter, skipped the big promised rural enrollment class my director wanted declared up front. It passed committee with zero fight. Nobody's enrollment numbers from those schools are going to move, same as the last two years. Was I wrong to leave the bold part out?

The vote on the admin fees is next Thursday and I haven't slept properly since I found out the numbers. I sit on the tenant panel at the agency, we're the ones who pushed to get the fees scrapped, the £45 they slap on you every time a rent payment bounces, plus the 'arrears letter' charges on top. The full motion would kill the fees completely and refund the last twelve months. It will lose. The owners have already told the panel chair it will lose. There's a watered-down version that caps the fees at £15 and scraps them entirely for anyone on housing benefit, and that one has the votes to actually pass.

Here's my problem. Through the panel I've got to know one of the tenants, a cleaner called Dana who had her hours cut last winter and is still paying off about £300 in fees from when she fell behind. Under the full motion she'd get all of it back. Under the capped version she gets nothing, she's not on benefits, she's just poor in the normal way, and the fees she's already paid stay paid. I've sat in her kitchen. I've seen the payment plan stuck to her fridge. She's asked me twice now how the vote is looking and I've changed the subject.

I keep thinking that if I vote for the capped version I'm voting to tell her, personally, that her £300 doesn't count. She'd be the one person I actually know who gets left behind by the thing I helped pass. Hundreds of other tenants would pay less going forward, I know that, I'm not stupid, but none of them have a face. She does. Everyone else on the panel is going to vote for the cap and I can already feel how good it would feel to be the one person in the room who didn't sell her out.

So do I vote against it? Tell me I'm not crazy for thinking that matters more than the arithmetic.

I voted against the fee cap at our tenant panel yesterday. It still passed without me, so tenants on benefits stop getting charged and everyone else's fees get capped, but my friend Dana, who's still paying off £300 of the old fees, gets nothing back, and I couldn't put my hand up for that. She's messaged me since asking how it went and I haven't replied.

Was I wrong?

I take the minutes for the tenant policy panel at the letting agency where I work. Next week they vote on scrapping the admin fees we charge tenants who fall behind on rent. Here's where it's landed: the full proposal, abolish the fees and refund the last twelve months, is dead, the owners will never sign it. There's a watered-down version that caps the fees and stops charging them to tenants on benefits, and that one has the votes. Everyone on the panel is treating it like a win.

Here's the thing I can't get past. Through the minutes and the front desk I've got to know one of our tenants, a cleaner, her hours got cut last winter, she's still paying off fees she was charged months ago. Under the full version she'd get that money back. Under the capped version she gets nothing. Not a penny. The refund is the whole point for people like her and it's the first thing that got traded away. So a room full of people who'll never pay one of these fees is going to pat itself on the back for a deal that leaves out exactly the people already drowning in them.

I don't have a vote, obviously, I just write down what they say. But I know most of the panel members and they do listen to me a bit because I'm the one who actually talks to tenants. I'm seriously thinking about telling the ones I know to vote the capped version down, force the owners to come back with something that includes the refunds. My colleague says that's insane, that you don't kill the only thing that can pass over the thing that can't, and that next year there might be no proposal at all. But it feels like if everyone keeps voting for half a loaf because the full loaf is 'unrealistic' then the full loaf is never even on the table. Am I wrong to want to push them to vote it down?

I told two people on our tenant panel yesterday that the capped fee deal is a sell-out and they should vote against it because it scraps the refunds. I just take the minutes, I don't get a vote. One of them looked at me like I'd spat on the table. Was I out of line?

Ten years I've chaired our parish council and last month was the first time I ever had to abandon a meeting. We've got the old village and then a newer estate on the edge of it, and for as long as anyone can remember the rec and the hall have gone to the same handful of village groups. Estate families rang up year after year and got told nothing was free. Last month about forty estate parents turned up, it turned into shouting, someone pulled the fire alarm, and we all went home.

Since then I've been trying to get a fair booking policy through. The old guard have the votes and they'll back it, but only if there's nothing in it saying the estate was kept out on purpose. No finding, nothing on the record, just a fresh start. The estate families want exactly that on the record. One of the mums said to me, if it gets written down as nobody's fault then you're saying it was fine to turn us away for ten years, and I didn't have an answer for her.

So I told both sides the finding stays or the policy doesn't come forward at all. My clerk thinks I've lost it. The policy is ready to go, Saturday slots for the estate kids' football, evening bookings at cost, all of it, and if I hold the line it dies and those kids carry on playing in the car park. The councillors won't budge either. One of them told me straight that he'd sooner nothing ever changed than stand up in that hall and say they froze people out. And I've got to say something about the meeting as well, because half the village wants the estate parents condemned and the other half wants a medal pinned on whoever pulled that alarm, and anything I say lands as one or the other.

I keep going round in circles. These families were turned away for years and everyone knew and nobody said a word. But I'm the one looking at the under-11s training in a car park in November.

Do I hold the line on the finding or put the policy forward without it?

I'm one of the estate parents. Last week I told the council we'd take the new booking policy even though they refused to put anything in writing saying we were shut out on purpose all those years. Kids get the hall and the pitch from January, that's real, that's Saturdays sorted. But half the estate is furious with me. They say I let the council write it up as a misunderstanding, like nobody ever did anything, and now there's nothing on record saying what actually happened to us. My own sister isn't speaking to me over it.

Was I wrong to take it?

I've chaired this club for six years and we're down to fielding one team most Saturdays, the bar takings don't cover the insurance, and we've lost every decent under-18 to the club two miles over because their facilities actually work. That club has now offered a full merger. Proper terms, our players keep their registrations, our committee people get roles, the name survives on the badge. But the deal means surrendering the lease on our ground, and the cottage on it goes back to the landlord. Mick lives in that cottage. He's kept our pitch for thirty years, he's sixty-three, his wife died in that house four years ago, and the job and the home are the same thing for him. There's no way a man his age gets another groundskeeping job with accommodation. I've run the numbers a hundred times and the club folds within two seasons without this merger, which means Mick loses the cottage anyway when we fold, just slower and with nothing to show for it. My committee would vote it down tomorrow because half of them haven't spoken to Mick in years and it's easy to be noble about a man you never see. I'd have to spend the next months persuading them, which means I believe in it, which means I've already decided Mick is a cost I'm willing to pay. There's no deadline on the offer so I can't even hide behind urgency. What do I actually do here?

I turned down the merger. Didn't even put it to the committee properly, just told the other club the timing wasn't right and let it go quiet. The deal would've saved us but it meant losing the ground, and our groundskeeper's cottage comes with the ground. He's sixty-three, widowed, thirty years with us. I couldn't do it to him. Now we've lost two more players and the treasurer says we've got maybe a year. Was I wrong?

The allotment committee votes tonight on turning six derelict plots into a community orchard and I've spent all week counting votes and it loses. It just loses. Derek has been against it for two years, calls it a land grab at every meeting, and he's got enough people who owe him favours from the water subcommittee to bury it. There's a smaller version floating around — three plots, two-year trial, rest deferred — and I'm fairly sure it passes but only if Derek himself votes for it, because his people follow his lead. I could get him there. I know I could. It would mean catching him before the meeting and framing it so he gets to present the trial as HIS idea, his conditions, his victory for careful stewardship, and I'd have to stand there and let him. Fine. I can swallow that. The part that's eating me is that to close it I'd basically have to tell him the other three plots are off the table, settled, done — and they're not, everyone knows land questions come back, I'd be saying it to make him safe. And the waiting families, the ones this whole thing is for, have already told me a three-plot trial is a sellout and I should go down fighting for all six. They'll get nothing if I go down fighting. Nothing. They don't have to sit across from Derek at the water meetings for the next decade though, I do, and maybe that's just me talking myself into the easy version. Do I take the three plots and eat the anger from the people I was trying to help, or is half a thing dressed up as a man's climbdown actually worse than losing honestly tonight?

I work dispatch at a regional ambulance centre, just a call-taker, no authority over anyone. For about a year the response times to the outlying villages have been getting worse and everyone knows why — we don't have enough vehicles. Some of us have been quietly fudging the triage codes to send ambulances to calls that technically don't qualify, because otherwise people out there wait forty minutes. Management's answer so far has been to draft up disciplinary measures. Now a senior manager has come to me privately, off the record, asking whether the floor would go along with a new package: rewritten triage protocol, a monitoring system to catch exactly the kind of rule-bending we've been doing, and zero new vehicles. She wants my answer in a few days before she takes it to the director, and whatever I say gets treated as what the whole floor thinks. The crews trust me and I know what they'll say — they'll say I'm selling them out if I touch it. But if I tell her no, nothing changes, the bending keeps going, the villages keep waiting, and sooner or later someone gets disciplined or someone out there dies waiting and both of those land on my conscience anyway. Part of me wants to tell her the package is fine IF she puts vehicles on the table, use the leverage, but she asked for a yes or no, not a negotiation, and I'm not a rep, I have no mandate to bargain for anyone. Do I give her a conditional answer, or flat no, or what — I keep going in circles and I have maybe three days.

Last night I told our senior manager the floor won't accept her new triage package without more ambulances in it. She asked me privately, I answered for everyone without asking anyone. Crews would back me but nobody gave me the right. The rule-bending and the slow village responses just carry on now. Did I do the right thing or did I just blow the only opening we had?

Three of them have now asked me straight out in the thread whether I’m shutting the group down, like I’m supposed to hand down a verdict while my brothers are still tearing chunks out of each other over £60 for petrol and who paid the cleaner. I set the whole thing up two years ago so Dad’s visits and meds and shopping didn’t fall through the cracks, and somehow I’ve ended up the admin everyone answers to and blames. My cousin left last night without a word, my sister who actually goes round there most says scrap the lot and start again, and I’m sitting here with a half-typed reply because if I write “I haven’t decided yet” they’ll all smell blood and pile in. Part of me wants to post something firm tonight — rota stands, money rows go private, anyone who wants out can say so to me not in the group — just to stop the bleeding and deal with whether the arrangement is even worth saving after Dad’s appointment on Friday. Do I send that now, or am I just putting a plaster on it because I can’t stand everyone watching me wobble?

I found out last week that our district nursing team is losing the double-staffed evening medication round. Budget decision, made two levels above us, not negotiable apparently. Some of our housebound patients will straight up miss their evening doses. There is a patient forum on Friday where relatives are going to ask us to our faces if evening visits are being cut, and I already know what the official line is going to be, some mush about 'restructuring to maintain quality of care.'

Here's where I'm at. I worked out that if I quietly give my team lead a list of the highest-risk patients, the ones who genuinely cannot miss a dose, she could probably protect just those visits. But only if it looks like her idea, like she's refining the plan, not like a junior nurse forced her into it. She's proud and she doesn't like me much. So the deal is: I hand her the list, I say nothing, the sickest people keep their meds, everyone else gets dropped, and she walks away looking good having conceded nothing.

Part of me wants to just stand up at that forum on Friday and answer the relatives honestly. Yes, the visits are being cut, yes, your mum is on the list of people who lose out, here's who made that decision. Because it's the truth and they're asking a person, not a press office. But the honest answer changes nobody's medication. It just frightens a room full of people and probably gets me managed out of the room for the rest of my career. The quiet option actually keeps insulin and heart meds going into actual bodies.

I keep going back and forth and Friday is coming fast. Do I take the list to her and keep my mouth shut at the forum, or do the relatives deserve someone in that room who will just say it plainly?

I've decided to pitch my team lead on protecting a short list of high-risk patients from the evening medication round cuts, and it only works if she thinks it's her own tweak to the plan, not a junior nurse pushing her. How do I word the ask so she can take the credit without me grovelling or making it obvious what I'm doing?

Four days ago the delivery app I drive for deactivated my account because a customer says their groceries never showed up. Except I have the doorstep photo, timestamped, GPS tag and everything, because I photograph every single drop. I've been through support three times now. Today they finally came back with an offer: they'll turn my account back on but the complaint stays on my record as a warning, and I get nothing for the four days of income I lost. Nothing. When I said I want the complaint removed, the lost week paid back, and an actual apology, they pasted the deactivation policy at me like I hadn't read it a hundred times already.

Here's the thing. This account is basically my whole income. Rent is due in five days and I'm short because of the days I already lost. Every hour I spend fighting with some chat agent who clearly has no power to give me anything is an hour I'm not earning. My brother keeps saying take the reinstatement, eat the warning, fight the rest later once money's coming in again. But I didn't do anything wrong and they know it, and if I accept a warning on my record for a delivery I have photographic proof of, what happens the next time some customer wants free groceries and files a claim? I'm one strike down already, through no fault of mine, and I'll be fighting to remove it from a position where I've already signed off on it.

I am so angry I can barely type. I want them to admit what they did. But I also need to pay rent. Do I take the deal or hold out for what they actually owe me?

I told the support agent they could keep their offer. Full reinstatement with a warning for a delivery I have timestamped photos of, no back pay, no apology? I said no and logged off. That was yesterday. Rent's due in four days and driving is my only income. Was I an idiot?

I work in the front office at my son's primary school, enrolments and waiting lists mostly, and there's a written policy that staff kids can come in from outside catchment, which is how my boy got in last year. Completely above board, it's in the staff handbook, anyone can read it. Now he's really struggling with reading, like properly behind, and there's one teacher everyone wants, she's got this reputation, so I asked the head if he could go in her class in September. She hasn't said no. She basically owes me a few favours and I think she'll do it. The problem is at parents' evening last week some mum stood up and had a go, didn't name me but everyone knew, about how office families always seem to land on their feet, and now a couple of the other parents are being funny with me at pickup. My thing is, the enrolment is policy, full stop, and the class thing is just the head being decent, which heads do all the time for all sorts of people. My son actually needs the help, that's the part nobody mentioning. He's seven and he cries over his reading book. Do I just leave it and hope the head still comes through, or do I go in and actually press the case before places are set? I keep going back and forth because if I push and she gets cold feet I don't want it to get weird, she's the one who signs off on everything round here. But if I say nothing I feel like I'm letting that woman's comment decide what my kid gets.

Quick one. I got my son into the school where I work using the staff enrolment policy, then asked the head for the teacher everyone wants, and she said yes. Another parent has now made a snide comment about staff families getting looked after. My son's behind on his reading and that teacher is meant to be the best. Was I actually out of line asking, or are people just annoyed it wasn't them?

I give Tuesday and Thursday nights to a charity-run hostel for seasonal orchard crews outside Renmark, and I drew up a plan for a shared dinner every week: a proper meal, the common room kept lit past ten, cards and phone credit and enough noise that nobody has to eat standing over a sink. Plenty of the pickers finish a shift and do not speak to another person until the next pay run. I priced the gas, the food, the insurance, the lot; the coordinator said it was the clearest note she had seen all year. Then she rang back and said the foundation board will only wear one dinner a month, and she would like me to put that smaller version forward when they meet because it can pass without an argument. Two board members have already called the weekly plan a comfort the hostel cannot carry.

This is the bit I cannot settle: am I being practical or gutless? A dinner each month is not nothing. People would drag themselves in for it. I can name the faces — there is a Samoan cutter who signs in for medical checks and then lingers by the washing machines because his demountable room is a bunk, a kettle and silence. He would be first through the door. So one voice in me says take the yes, cook well, let the room fill up, and maybe the budget grows once they see boots under the tables. That is how small things become permanent, surely.

Except I asked for every week because the ache is every week. Being alone does not wait for the first Friday of the month. And if I stand there and describe the monthly dinner as my plan, I am letting them believe I overstated the need, when I do not think I did. The coordinator keeps telling me this is how money moves in this world; she has survived twenty budgets and I have been around since the blossom. Maybe the smart thing is to shut up and learn. They sit a week from Friday. Do I put the monthly dinner forward as mine, or not?

After close on Monday I pulled Mara into the back office and told her the panel would only hear the travel pot if she trimmed it to the page that pays for maybe one case in three, the draft that slides through. She started that pot after Noor lost his appeal slot in spring because the ride to the tribunal cost more than he had until payday; since then she has a folder of letters, dates, fares, missed calls, and even the capped version comes to less than our coffee budget. Two panel members have already warned me the larger ask is dead, one with that tight smile people use for broken boilers. The packet lands Friday and I told Mara I need the lean draft by midday so there is no space for debate. I keep thinking I should take the win, protect at least Noor's cousin and the family from the camp, and call it strategy. But she has already let two people believe a yes might be near, and if I make her shrink it I am not just saving the pot; I am handing her the pen and asking her to mark whose door stays shut. When she asks what figure to put on the first line, do I tell her to write the sum she actually costed, or the smaller one I said would survive?
